analysis.one_liner: Replaces bank-issued, government-guaranteed student loans with loans made directly by the federal government, with income-based repayment.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 1993, the bill was sent to a House subcommittee on May 27 and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would phase out the Federal Family Education Loan program, in which private banks make student loans with federal guarantees and subsidies, and replace it with loans made directly by the Department of Education over four years. Students could repay through a standard plan or a new income-based "EXCEL Account" plan, with interest-rate caps and no school-charged origination fees. The goal stated in the bill is to cut the cost and confusion of routing federal loans through private middlemen.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers and taxpayers. Borrowers would get one loan source, capped interest rates, a menu of repayment plans including one pegged to income, and a ban on school-charged origination fees. Taxpayers would stop paying interest subsidies and guarantee payments to private lenders. Colleges would also gain, since the Education Secretary would pay them fees to originate loans.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs a four-year phase-in in which direct federal lending would go from 4 percent of new loan volume in 1994-95 to 100 percent by 1997-98, fully replacing the guaranteed-loan program.

Borrowers could choose standard, extended, graduated, or income-contingent repayment through an "EXCEL Account" whose payments are based on adjusted gross income, so low earners in community-service careers would not be locked out by fixed payments.
Direct loans would carry capped interest rates (9 percent for Stafford loans, 10 percent for parent PLUS loans, 11 percent for supplemental loans) with lower lender margins after mid-1997.
Schools would be barred from charging students any origination fees, and the Education Secretary would pay institutions a fee (starting near $10 per borrower) for originating loans.
The bill authorizes a plan for repaying loans through IRS wage withholding and lets the IRS disclose limited tax data to the Education Department to set income-based payment amounts.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, private lenders, guaranty agencies, and Sallie Mae would lose a government-backed business built on federal guarantees and interest subsidies. Borrowers would still pay a loan fee of 5 to 6.5 percent and their loans would remain undischargeable in bankruptcy. The federal government would take on the full administrative job, funded at up to $749 million by fiscal 1998.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private lenders, guaranty agencies, Sallie Mae

drawbacks.text: Student loans would remain nondischargeable in bankruptcy, keeping one of the harshest features of the existing system in place even as delivery was reformed.
Borrowers would be charged a loan fee of not less than 5 percent and not more than 6.5 percent of the loan principal.

Income-based repayment would rely on the IRS disclosing taxpayer identity, filing status, and adjusted gross income to the Education Department, and possibly on IRS wage withholding, raising privacy concerns about tax data use.

The bill concentrates the entire federal student loan function in the Department of Education, with administrative and transition funding rising to $749 million in fiscal 1998 — a real implementation risk for a program covering 100 percent of loan volume within four years.

The bill itself builds transition safeguards, such as requiring Sallie Mae to serve as lender of last resort, which is an implicit acknowledgment that a rapid shift to full direct lending could disrupt loan access for students at schools not yet in the program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but lopsided: direct lending would cut out a middleman layer that costs taxpayers subsidies and fees, while giving borrowers simpler, cheaper, more flexible loans. The bill's own costs — bankruptcy protections kept off the table, a 5-6.5 percent borrower fee, IRS access to tax data, and a compressed four-year transition — are genuine but secondary to that main shift. As drafted, it helps ordinary borrowers far more than it threatens anyone outside the guaranteed-loan industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to its subcommittee on postsecondary education, where it sat with no markup or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert E. Andrews (D-NJ) introduced the Student Loan Reform Act of 1993 on May 11, 1993, with 11 Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced, and on May 27, 1993 to the Subcommittee on Postsecondary Education and Training.
The action history lists no further steps — no subcommittee vote, no committee markup, no floor action — through the end of the 103rd Congress in January 1995.

The bill's stated goal was to replace the Federal Family Education Loan program, in which the government guarantees loans made by private lenders, with a Federal Direct Student Loan program phased in over four years to 100 percent of new loan volume.

Later in 1993, a direct lending program was enacted as part of that year's budget reconciliation law, but only in a phased, capped form that preserved the guaranteed-loan system alongside it — the full four-year phase-out this bill proposed was never adopted.
The guaranteed-loan industry, including lenders, guaranty agencies, and Sallie Mae, campaigned during the 1993 reauthorization to limit direct lending and preserve its federally backed role.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student loan lenders, guaranty agencies, and Sallie Mae kept their government-guaranteed business; the full phase-out this bill proposed was never voted on, and students got direct lending only in a smaller, slower form enacted separately.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Guaranteed-loan lenders, guaranty agencies, Sallie Mae

industries.industry: Private student loan lenders (Federal Family Education Loan program)
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated, by 1998, the system under which private lenders make student loans with federal guarantees and interest subsidies paid by taxpayers. Taxpayers and borrowers currently fund that middleman layer; the bill would have routed loans directly through the Education Department instead.

The bill terminates the agencies' administrative cost allowance after fiscal 1993, lets the Education Secretary terminate their agreements and assume their functions, and declares their reserve funds federal property. Their core role — guaranteeing privately made loans for a government-paid fee — would disappear as direct lending phased in.

As a government-sponsored enterprise that buys guaranteed student loans, Sallie Mae's core market would shrink to zero under full direct lending. The bill would require it to serve only as a transition-period lender of last resort and directs a study of converting it to a private corporation.
Servicing and collection work would continue, but under Education Department contracts rather than within the guarantee system, with potentially different volumes and fee structures.
Participating institutions would be paid origination fees by the Education Secretary and barred from charging borrowers any fees, giving schools a new administrative revenue stream.
